newsitem.title: FRANCE: French SNCF rail unions growl at 1997 pay offer.
newsitem.headline: French SNCF rail unions growl at 1997 pay offer.

text.p: The two biggest trade unions in France's SNCF state railways said on Thursday an offer of a 1.0 percent general pay rise in two stages for 1997 was not enough and risked exacerbating labour tensions in the coming months.

The Communist-led CGT and Socialist CFDT, which represent a large majority of SNCF employees, said they had been offered a rise of 0.5 percent in April followed by another 0.5 percent in September at a meeting with management.
The pay offer was well below forecast inflation, as had been the pay rise in 1996, they said.
The CGT said in a statement it was unhappy with the offer and that it would provide a platform for a united stand by rail workers. It would consult members on Friday on the matter.

Both the CGT and the CFDT have been campaigning against reform of the railways but occasional strike calls have so far failed to generate anything like the crippling three-week stoppage of late 1995 over a now-defunct government attack on early pension rights.

The CFDT, the second largest union in the railways after the CGT, also attacked the pay offer and said it appeared to have been prepared precisely in line with the framework established by the SNCF's ultimate mentors, the government.
"At a time when all the talk is about the challenges the SNCF must meet, the rail workers have once again been left on the platform," the CFDT said in its own statement.
"No doubt the SNCF management's decision on salaries will take its toll in the coming weeks on the level of conflict," it added.
The CFDT said salaries rose 1.7 percent in 1996, below the 1.8 percent rate of inflation and that this year's one percent rise fell even shorter of a predicted 1.5 percent rate of inflation.
"Once again these measures will mean a loss in purchasing power for both active and retired rail workers," it said. "Far from closing the gaps of the preceding years, this will amplify them."
The Force Ouvriere union also issued a statement saying its initial reaction was negative but that it would decide in the coming days whether to sign the pay offer.
